isa-assembly-001.question: Which statement is correct about two CPUs that implement the same instruction set architecture (ISA)?
choices: They are built with the same circuits, so their performance and power are the same
Even if their internal circuits differ, they can run the same machine-code program
They must be made in the same fab using the same process
isa-assembly-001.explanation: An ISA is the contract between software and hardware that defines the kinds of instructions, their bit layout, the number of registers and so on. The internal organization, such as the number of pipeline stages, the cache sizes and the branch predictor, is called the microarchitecture and is chosen separately from the ISA. So one ISA can have both small low-power cores and large high-performance cores that differ in speed and power yet run the same machine code. The fab and process have nothing to do with the ISA.
choiceNotes: The circuit organization (microarchitecture) differs between products.
Correct. The ISA is a contract; the implementation is free.
An ISA says nothing about how chips are manufactured.

isa-assembly-002.question: What is a characteristic of a load-store architecture such as RISC-V?
choices: Arithmetic instructions such as add read values directly from memory and write results back to memory
Only load and store instructions access memory; arithmetic is done between registers
It has no registers and computes by pushing all values onto a stack
isa-assembly-002.explanation: In a load-store architecture, a memory value is first loaded into a register, arithmetic such as add or compare is done between registers, and results are written back to memory with a store if needed. Because arithmetic instructions never touch memory, instructions have a uniform shape and are easy to pipeline. This contrasts with designs like x86, where an arithmetic instruction such as "add eax, [mem]" can read memory.
choiceNotes: Arithmetic instructions operating on memory is a CISC trait, as in x86.
Correct. Memory access is limited to loads and stores.
That is a stack machine, not a load-store design.

isa-assembly-003.question: What is the property of register x0 (zero) in RISC-V?
choices: It always reads as 0, and writes to it have no effect
It holds the return address of a function
It acts as a flag showing whether the last result was zero
isa-assembly-003.explanation: x0 always returns 0, and writes to it are ignored. Having the constant 0 always available lets "add rd, rs, x0" copy a value, "addi rd, x0, 5" set a constant, and a destination of x0 discard a result, without extra dedicated instructions. The return address goes in x1 (ra). RISC-V has no result flags; branch instructions compare two registers directly.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is a constant-zero register.
The return address goes in x1 (ra).
RISC-V has no flag register for results.

isa-assembly-004.question: Which describes the general-purpose integer registers of RISC-V RV32I (the 32-bit base integer instruction set)?
choices: 32 registers (x0-x31), each 32 bits wide
8 registers (x0-x7), each 32 bits wide
64 registers (x0-x63), each 64 bits wide
isa-assembly-004.explanation: RV32I has 32 integer registers, x0 to x31, each 32 bits wide (the 64-bit RV64I widens them to 64 bits but keeps 32 registers). The register field in an instruction is 5 bits, which can name 2^5 = 32 registers. They also have aliases such as ra, sp and a0, whose roles are set by the calling convention. For embedded use there is RV32E with only 16 registers.
choiceNotes: Correct. x0-x31, with x0 always 0.
Eight is close to the count of general registers in 32-bit x86.
Even the 64-bit RV64I has 32 registers.

isa-assembly-005.question: What is the relationship between assembly language and machine code?
choices: Assembly instructions are translated almost one-to-one into machine instructions by an assembler
Assembly is the same for every CPU and runs unchanged on any of them
Machine code is an interpreter that reads assembly line by line at run time
isa-assembly-005.explanation: Assembly language writes machine instructions as readable mnemonics such as "add a0, a0, a1", and an assembler converts them into instruction bit patterns. Because it maps almost one-to-one onto instructions, a different ISA means a different assembly language. Pseudo-instructions such as "li" and "mv", however, are replaced by the assembler with one or more real instructions. Turning labels into addresses is also the assembler's job.
choiceNotes: Correct. It writes the instructions as readable mnemonics.
Assembly differs for each ISA.
Machine code is the bit pattern the CPU executes directly.

isa-assembly-006.question: Which real instruction does the assembler use for the RISC-V pseudo-instruction "nop" (do nothing)?
choices: addi x0, x0, 0
jal ra, 0
lw x0, 0(sp)
isa-assembly-006.explanation: RISC-V has no dedicated do-nothing instruction; nop is encoded as "addi x0, x0, 0". The write to x0 is discarded, so no register or memory changes. Likewise "mv rd, rs" is "addi rd, rs, 0", "j label" is "jal x0, label" and "ret" is "jalr x0, 0(ra)". Using x0 to keep the number of instruction kinds small is part of the RISC-V design philosophy.
choiceNotes: Correct. An add whose result is discarded into x0.
It overwrites ra, so it is not a no-op.
It reads memory and could even raise an exception.

isa-assembly-007.question: What is the difference between the RISC-V "add" and "addi" instructions?
choices: add adds integers; addi adds floating-point numbers
add adds values in memory; addi adds register values
add adds two registers; addi adds a register and a constant written in the instruction (an immediate)
isa-assembly-007.explanation: "add rd, rs1, rs2" puts the sum of two registers into rd, and "addi rd, rs1, imm" adds a register and a 12-bit constant (an immediate) embedded in the instruction. An immediate saves the step of first loading the constant into a register. RISC-V has no subtract-immediate instruction; it subtracts by adding a negative immediate, as in "addi t0, t0, -1".
choiceNotes: Floating-point addition uses separate instructions such as fadd.s.
RISC-V arithmetic never accesses memory directly.
Correct. The i stands for immediate.

isa-assembly-008.question: After running the RISC-V code above, what is the value in register a2?
isa-assembly-008.explanation: Line 1 adds 5 to zero (always 0), giving a0 = 5; line 2 adds 3 to a0, giving a1 = 8; line 3 adds a0 and a1, giving a2 = 5 + 8 = 13. RISC-V arithmetic is written "op destination, source1, source2 (or immediate)", so the first register is where the result goes. zero is an alias of x0 and is often used to build constants.
choiceNotes: 8 is the value of a1.
Correct. 5 + 8 = 13.
Recheck a1: it is 5 + 3 = 8.

isa-assembly-009.question: What does the RISC-V instruction "lw t0, 8(sp)" do?
choices: Writes the 4 bytes of t0 to the address sp + 8
Reads 4 bytes from the address sp + 8 and puts them in t0
Reads 4 bytes from the address sp × 8 and puts them in t0
isa-assembly-009.explanation: lw stands for load word and reads 32 bits (4 bytes) from memory. "8(sp)" means the address formed by adding 8 to sp as a base; this way of specifying an address is called base-plus-offset (register indirect with displacement). It is convenient for reaching stack variables or struct members at a fixed distance from a base. The opposite, writing a register to memory, is sw (store word).
choiceNotes: Writing is done with the sw instruction.
Correct. It loads from base register plus offset.
The offset is added, not multiplied.

isa-assembly-010.question: In the RISC-V conditional branch "beq a0, a1, label", how is the target address of label encoded?
choices: The full 32-bit target address is held in the instruction
As a distance from the address (PC) of the branch instruction itself, held in the instruction
The target address must be placed in register a1 beforehand
isa-assembly-010.explanation: RISC-V branches encode the target as a signed distance in bytes from the address (PC) of the current instruction. This is called PC-relative addressing. Branch targets are usually nearby, so a short distance suffices and fits within the 32-bit instruction. And because the distance stays the same if the whole program is placed at another address, the code works without being rewritten.
choiceNotes: A 32-bit address cannot fit in a 32-bit instruction.
Correct. This is PC-relative addressing.
a1 is one of the values compared, not an address.

isa-assembly-011.question: What is an advantage of using PC-relative addressing for branches and jumps?
choices: The branch can always reach any target with one instruction, however far
Branch prediction becomes unnecessary and the pipeline never stalls
The program runs without modifying its instructions no matter where in memory it is loaded
isa-assembly-011.explanation: A PC-relative branch states its target as "so many bytes from here", so if the whole program is shifted to another address the distance is unchanged and it still works. This is the foundation of position-independent code (PIC) used in shared libraries. The distance field has limited bits, though, so far jumps combine auipc and jalr. The need for branch prediction is unrelated to how the target is encoded.
choiceNotes: The immediate field is limited, so the reach is limited.
How the target is encoded has nothing to do with branch prediction.
Correct. It makes position-independent code easy.

isa-assembly-012.question: Which statement about instruction length in the RISC-V base ISA and in x86 is correct?
choices: Both use a fixed 32-bit length
RISC-V is variable-length and x86 is a fixed 32 bits
RISC-V base instructions are a fixed 32 bits; x86 instructions vary from 1 to 15 bytes
isa-assembly-012.explanation: All RISC-V base instructions are 32 bits, so instruction boundaries are obvious (the compressed C extension mixes in 16-bit instructions). x86 ranges from 1-byte instructions up to 15 bytes including prefixes and immediates, and the start of the next instruction is unknown until the current one is decoded. As a result, decoding several x86 instructions at once requires complex circuitry.
choiceNotes: x86 is not fixed-length.
It is the other way around.
Correct. x86 lengths vary because of decades of extensions.

isa-assembly-013.question: What is the main advantage of making instructions a fixed length?
choices: Instruction boundaries are known immediately, making it easy to decode several instructions at once
Every instruction is shorter than variable-length ones, so programs always get smaller
The number of instruction types can grow without limit
isa-assembly-013.explanation: With fixed length, the nth instruction always starts at byte 4n, so many instructions can be fetched and decoded in parallel. This especially helps superscalar CPUs that issue several instructions per cycle. On the other hand, common instructions cannot be made shorter, so code tends to be larger than with variable-length encodings. The RISC-V C extension adds 16-bit instructions to offset this weakness.
choiceNotes: Correct. The decoder becomes simpler.
Variable-length encodings, which can shorten common instructions, usually give smaller code.
A fixed number of bits limits how many instructions can be encoded.

isa-assembly-014.question: In RISC-V instructions, each register field (rd, rs1, rs2) is 5 bits wide. Why?
choices: Because the registers are 5 bits wide
Because one instruction can use up to five registers
There are 32 integer registers, and 2^5 = 32 values can name each of them
isa-assembly-014.explanation: An R-type instruction consists, from the top, of funct7 (7 bits), rs2 (5), rs1 (5), funct3 (3), rd (5) and opcode (7), 32 bits in total. With 32 registers, a register number fits in 5 bits. Going to 64 registers would need 6 bits per field, 3 extra bits for three fields, leaving fewer bits for immediates and opcodes. The number of registers is tied to the instruction format.
choiceNotes: Registers are 32 or 64 bits wide.
Base instructions use at most three registers: rd, rs1 and rs2.
Correct. Five bits encode 0 to 31.

isa-assembly-015.question: The immediate of RISC-V addi is a 12-bit signed integer. What range can it represent?
isa-assembly-015.explanation: A 12-bit two's complement value ranges from -2^11 = -2048 to 2^11 - 1 = 2047. The immediate is sign-extended to 32 bits (64 on RV64) before use, so negative numbers can be added directly. To use a constant beyond this range, several instructions are combined, for example setting the upper 20 bits with lui and then adding the lower 12 bits with addi.
choiceNotes: That is the unsigned 12-bit range.
Correct. The 12-bit two's complement range.
That range needs 13 bits.

isa-assembly-016.question: In RISC-V, what is the usual way to put a 32-bit constant that does not fit in a 12-bit immediate (e.g. 0x12345678) into a register?
choices: Use a single addi with the whole 32-bit immediate
Set the upper 20 bits with lui, then add the lower 12 bits with addi
Constants cannot be used, so the value must always be read from input
isa-assembly-016.explanation: lui (load upper immediate) places a 20-bit immediate in bits 31-12 of a register and clears the low 12 bits. Following it with addi to add the low 12 bits produces any 32-bit constant. Writing "li a0, 0x12345678" in assembly makes the assembler expand it into these two instructions as needed. In fixed-length ISAs, building large constants in pieces is the norm.
choiceNotes: A 32-bit immediate cannot fit in a 32-bit instruction.
Correct. The li pseudo-instruction expands to this pair.
Two instructions build it, or it can be loaded from memory.

isa-assembly-017.question: To build the constant 0x12345FFF in RISC-V with lui and addi, which pair is correct?
choices: lui t0, 0x12346 followed by addi t0, t0, -1
lui t0, 0x12345 followed by addi t0, t0, 0xFFF
lui t0, 0x12345 followed by addi t0, t0, -1
isa-assembly-017.explanation: The addi immediate is sign-extended, so when the low 12 bits are 0xFFF (top bit set) it is added as -1. The upper part built by lui is therefore made one larger, 0x12346, and adding -1 to 0x12346000 yields 0x12345FFF. This correction, adding 1 to the upper part whenever bit 11 of the low part is set, is done automatically by assemblers and linkers.
choiceNotes: The 12-bit value 0xFFF is sign-extended and added as -1.
That gives 0x12345000 - 1 = 0x12344FFF.

isa-assembly-018.question: What does the RISC-V auipc instruction (add upper immediate to PC) do?
choices: Stores the PC value directly to memory
Adds the 20-bit immediate shifted left by 12 bits to its own address (PC) and puts the result in a register
Jumps unconditionally to the address given by the immediate, overwriting the PC
isa-assembly-018.explanation: auipc simply puts PC + (immediate << 12) into a register. Following it with jalr or lw that add a low 12-bit offset lets code name a function or data item within about ±2 GiB of the current position as a distance from the PC. This allows position-independent code, which runs wherever it is loaded, to call distant functions and read global variables.
choiceNotes: It does not store to memory.
Correct. It builds PC-relative addresses.
auipc itself does not jump.

isa-assembly-019.question: On RISC-V RV32I, what 32-bit value is in t0 after "addi t0, zero, -1"?
choices: 0xFFFFFFFF
0x00000FFF
isa-assembly-019.explanation: The immediate -1 is 0xFFF in 12 bits. addi sign-extends it to 32 bits, copying the top bit of 1 into every higher bit, giving 0xFFFFFFFF, which is -1 in two's complement. Thanks to sign extension, adding a negative immediate performs subtraction. Filling the upper bits with zeros would give 0x00000FFF = 4095, a different meaning.
choiceNotes: Correct. -1 is sign-extended to all ones.
That is the value if zero-filled instead of sign-extended.
That is -1 in sign-magnitude, not two's complement.

isa-assembly-020.question: A byte in memory holds 0x80. Which pair correctly gives the 32-bit register value after loading it with RISC-V lb and with lbu?
choices: lb gives 0x00000080 (128); lbu gives 0xFFFFFF80 (-128)
lb gives 0xFFFFFF80 (-128); lbu gives 0x00000080 (128)
isa-assembly-020.explanation: lb (load byte) treats the byte as signed and copies its top bit into the upper 24 bits (sign extension). 0x80 has a top bit of 1, so the result is 0xFFFFFF80, which is -128. lbu (load byte unsigned) fills the upper bits with zeros (zero extension), giving 128. When C code reads a signed char versus an unsigned char, the compiler chooses between these two instructions.
choiceNotes: The u means unsigned, so this is reversed.
Correct. lb sign-extends; lbu zero-extends.
lb spreads the top bit of 1 upward.

isa-assembly-021.question: How do RISC-V and x86 differ in their mechanism for conditional branches?
choices: RISC-V branches on flags; x86 branches compare two registers directly
Neither has conditional branches; both choose targets with a lookup table
In RISC-V the branch compares two registers directly; in x86 the branch tests flags set by a compare instruction
isa-assembly-021.explanation: In x86, "cmp eax, ebx" compares and sets flags (condition codes) such as zero and carry, and the following "je" or "jl" branches on those flags. RISC-V has no flags; the branch itself compares two registers, as in "beq a0, a1, L" or "blt a0, a1, L". With no implicit state like flags, dependences are easier to track when instructions are reordered or executed in parallel.
choiceNotes: It is the other way around.
Both have conditional branch instructions.
Correct. RISC-V compares and branches in one instruction.

isa-assembly-022.question: What does the RISC-V instruction "slt t0, a0, a1" do?
choices: Shifts a0 left by a1 bits and puts the result in t0
Branches to the address in t0 if a0 is less than a1
Puts 1 in t0 if a0 is less than a1, otherwise 0
isa-assembly-022.explanation: slt (set less than) compares two registers as signed integers and writes 1 if the first is smaller, otherwise 0. There are also sltu for unsigned comparison and slti for comparison with an immediate. It is used when a comparison result is needed as a value, as in C's "x = (a < b);", or to replace a branch with arithmetic. Shifts are sll and branches are separate instructions such as blt.
choiceNotes: Shift left is the sll instruction.
slt does not branch.
Correct. It stands for set less than.

isa-assembly-023.question: When the RISC-V code above finishes, what is the value in t0?
isa-assembly-023.explanation: The loop adds t1 to t0 while decreasing t1 from 4 by one each time. t0 becomes 4, 7, 9 and 10, and when t1 reaches 0, bnez (branch if not zero) no longer branches and the loop exits. The result is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. bnez is a pseudo-instruction for "bne t1, zero, loop". Counting down to zero is common because no constant is needed for the comparison.
choiceNotes: The loop runs more than once.
Include the addition when t1 = 1.

isa-assembly-024.question: RISC-V conditional branches (B-type) encode the distance as a 13-bit signed byte offset whose lowest bit is always 0 and not stored. Roughly what range can a branch reach directly?
choices: About 4 KiB before or after the branch
About 1 MiB before or after the branch
Anywhere in memory
isa-assembly-024.explanation: A 13-bit signed value covers -4096 to +4095, but instructions are aligned on 2-byte boundaries, so the lowest bit is always 0 and the range is -4096 to +4094 bytes. Omitting that bit doubles the reach for the same field size. For a more distant target, the assembler rewrites the code as a short branch on the inverted condition that skips over a jal, which reaches about ±1 MiB.
choiceNotes: Correct. -4096 to +4094 bytes.
About 1 MiB is the reach of jal (21 bits).
A limited number of bits cannot cover all of memory.

isa-assembly-025.question: What does the RISC-V instruction "jal ra, func" do?
choices: Saves the address of the next instruction in ra, then jumps to func
Only puts the address of func in ra and does not jump
Returns to the address held in ra
isa-assembly-025.explanation: jal (jump and link) writes the address of the next instruction (PC + 4) into the given register (the link) and jumps to the target. The calling convention puts the return address in ra (x1), so a call is written "jal ra, func", or "call func" as a pseudo-instruction. The called function returns to the address in ra when it finishes. With x0 as the destination, jal becomes a plain jump.
choiceNotes: Correct. This is the call instruction.
jal also jumps.
Returning is done by ret (jalr).

isa-assembly-026.question: Which real instruction executes the RISC-V pseudo-instruction "ret"?
choices: jal ra, 0
jalr x0, 0(ra)
lw ra, 0(sp)
isa-assembly-026.explanation: jalr (jump and link register) jumps to a register value plus an offset and writes the next instruction's address into the destination. ret is "jalr x0, 0(ra)": it jumps to the address in ra and discards the link in x0. jalr is also used for jumps whose target is decided at run time, such as calls through function pointers or virtual functions. Restoring ra with "lw ra, ..." is preparation done before ret.
choiceNotes: It overwrites ra, so it cannot return.
Correct. It jumps to ra and discards the link.
It only loads ra from memory and does not return.

isa-assembly-027.question: What is the main purpose of defining a calling convention?
choices: To standardize function names and make programs readable
So that separately compiled functions and libraries can pass arguments and return values correctly
To require OS permission each time a function is called
isa-assembly-027.explanation: A calling convention specifies which registers hold arguments, where return values go, which registers the callee may clobber and how the stack is used. Because of this agreement, libraries built by different compilers, or assembly functions combined with C functions, work together correctly. The calling convention is a key part of the ABI (application binary interface).
choiceNotes: It is not a naming rule.
Correct. It is a machine-level agreement.
The OS is not involved in function calls.

isa-assembly-028.question: In the standard RISC-V calling convention, which registers pass integer arguments and return values?
choices: Arguments in s0-s7; return value in ra
Arguments in a0-a7; return value in a0 (and a1)
All arguments on the stack; return value in sp
isa-assembly-028.explanation: In the standard RISC-V calling convention, up to eight integer arguments are passed in a0-a7 (x10-x17), and the return value comes back in a0, or in a0 and a1 for values such as 64-bit integers on RV32. Passing through registers, which are faster than memory, keeps call overhead low. Arguments beyond eight go on the stack. Floating-point arguments use fa0-fa7.
choiceNotes: s registers are saved registers; ra is the return address.
Correct. The a stands for argument.
Up to eight go in registers; sp is the stack position.

isa-assembly-029.question: In the standard RISC-V calling convention, when calling a function with ten integer arguments, where are the ninth and tenth passed?
choices: In s0 and s1
In t0 and t1
On the stack
isa-assembly-029.explanation: There are only eight argument registers, a0-a7, so from the ninth argument on the caller places them on the stack and the callee reads them at fixed positions relative to the stack pointer. The extra memory accesses make functions with very many arguments a little slower. Passing a pointer to a struct instead of many separate values is a common way to keep the argument count down.
choiceNotes: s registers are callee-saved, not for arguments.
t registers are temporaries, not for arguments.
Correct. Whatever does not fit in registers goes on the stack.

isa-assembly-030.question: In the RISC-V calling convention, s0-s11 are callee-saved registers. What does that mean?
choices: If the called function uses them, it must save the old values and restore them before returning
The calling function must clear them all to 0 before the call
Only the OS may use them; user programs cannot
isa-assembly-030.explanation: Callee-saved registers are guaranteed to keep their values across a call. If the called function wants to use s0 or another s register, it saves it on the stack at entry and restores it before returning. The caller can keep values it still needs after the call in s registers without saving them itself. Loop variables are often placed there.
choiceNotes: Correct. To the caller their values appear preserved.
There is no rule to clear them.
User programs use them normally.

isa-assembly-031.question: In the RISC-V calling convention, t0-t6 are caller-saved. If a function wants to keep using a value in t0 after calling another function, what should it do?
choices: Nothing; the called function always restores t0
Nothing; other functions cannot modify t0
Save t0 to the stack or elsewhere before the call and restore it after
isa-assembly-031.explanation: The callee may use t registers freely without saving them. So if the value is needed after the call, the caller must save it itself. Splitting the saving responsibility between caller and callee, register by register, lets most functions use temporaries with no saving work and reduces the total number of saves and restores.
choiceNotes: The callee may freely overwrite t registers.
Any function may use t0 freely.
Correct. Or keep it in an s register in the first place.

isa-assembly-032.question: A function that calls no other functions (a leaf function) often does not need to save ra on the stack. Why?
choices: Because leaf functions do not use the ret instruction
Because the CPU automatically pushes the return address of leaf functions
Because it calls no one, ra is never overwritten and the return address stays intact
isa-assembly-032.explanation: Every jal overwrites ra, so a function that calls others must first save its own return address on the stack. A leaf function never executes jal, so ra stays intact and it can ret without saving it. If it also avoids callee-saved registers, it does not even need a stack frame. x86's call instruction always pushes the return address on the stack, which is a difference from RISC-V.
choiceNotes: Leaf functions also return with ret.
RISC-V jal only writes a register; it does not push to the stack.
Correct. It never executes a jal that would overwrite ra.

isa-assembly-033.question: What is the purpose of executing "addi sp, sp, -16" at the start of a RISC-V function?
choices: To grow the stack toward lower addresses and reserve a 16-byte work area
To free 16 bytes on the stack
To subtract 16 from sp and return it as the result
isa-assembly-033.explanation: By the convention of many ISAs, RISC-V included, the stack grows from higher toward lower addresses. Subtracting 16 from sp makes the 16 bytes between the new sp and the old one this function's stack frame, where the return address, saved registers and local variables can be kept. At the end, "addi sp, sp, 16" restores sp and frees the area, returning to the state before the call.
choiceNotes: Correct. The stack grows toward lower addresses.
Freeing is the final "addi sp, sp, 16".
Return values go in a0.

isa-assembly-034.question: The standard RISC-V calling convention requires sp to be a multiple of 16 bytes on function entry. What is the main reason?
choices: Because the OS will not boot unless the stack size is a multiple of 16 bytes
Because the low 4 bits of sp record the function number
So that data up to 16 bytes placed on the stack can be accessed efficiently without crossing alignment boundaries
isa-assembly-034.explanation: Data placed at an address that is a multiple of its size (aligned) can be accessed in one operation without crossing a boundary. Keeping sp a multiple of 16 preserves alignment for 8-byte doubles or 16-byte long doubles placed on the stack. So functions allocate frames in multiples of 16 bytes, using "addi sp, sp, -16" even if they save only one register.
choiceNotes: It has nothing to do with booting the OS.
No information is stored in the low bits of sp.
Correct. It keeps double-precision and 128-bit data aligned.

isa-assembly-035.question: The code above is the start (prologue) of a function. What does it do?
choices: It reserves stack space and saves the return address (ra) and the callee-saved s0
It loads the function arguments ra and s0 from the stack
It frees the stack in order to return from the function
isa-assembly-035.explanation: Line 1 subtracts 16 from sp to allocate a stack frame, line 2 writes the return address ra into it, and line 3 writes the callee-saved s0. The function calls other functions, so it must protect ra, and it uses s0, so it must preserve s0's old value. The epilogue at the end reverses this with "lw s0, 8(sp)", "lw ra, 12(sp)", "addi sp, sp, 16" and "ret".
choiceNotes: Correct. The epilogue undoes this in reverse.
sw is a store, and neither ra nor s0 is an argument.
sp is decreased, so this is allocation.

isa-assembly-036.question: What is an advantage of using a frame pointer (s0/fp in RISC-V) inside a function?
choices: It avoids using an extra register, so performance always improves
Locals and arguments can be addressed at fixed offsets even if sp moves, and debuggers can walk the call chain easily
The stack grows automatically and never overflows
isa-assembly-036.explanation: A frame pointer is a register that keeps pointing at the stack position on function entry and does not move. Even if sp changes partway, for example with variable-length arrays, locals can be addressed as "so many bytes from fp". And if each frame stores the previous fp, following them yields the call chain (a backtrace). It does occupy one register, though, so optimized code often omits it.
choiceNotes: On the contrary, it dedicates one register.
Correct. It serves as the frame's fixed reference point.
It does nothing to prevent stack overflow.

isa-assembly-037.question: In RISC-V, what happens if a recursive function (one that calls itself) forgets to save ra on the stack?
choices: The inner call overwrites ra, so the outer invocation cannot return to its real caller
Nothing goes wrong, because the CPU saves ra automatically
The result is doubled regardless of recursion depth
isa-assembly-037.explanation: The recursive jal overwrites ra with "the instruction after my own call". If ra was not saved, when the outer invocation executes ret it returns into itself instead of to its original caller, looping or misbehaving. That is why any function that calls another must save ra on the stack in its prologue and restore it in its epilogue.
choiceNotes: Correct. It keeps returning to just after its own jal.
RISC-V jal only overwrites ra.
The result is not scaled by a fixed factor.

isa-assembly-038.question: On little-endian RISC-V, a register holding 0x12345678 is stored with sw to address 0x100. What value does lbu then read from address 0x101?
isa-assembly-038.explanation: Little-endian places the bytes of a value in ascending addresses starting from the least significant. For 0x12345678, address 0x100 holds 0x78, 0x101 holds 0x56, 0x102 holds 0x34 and 0x103 holds 0x12. So the byte at 0x101 is 0x56. In big-endian the order would be 0x12, 0x34, ... from 0x100, and 0x101 would hold 0x34. The difference matters when handling network or file formats.
choiceNotes: 0x34 is at address 0x102.
Correct. It is the second-lowest byte.
0x78 is at address 0x100.

isa-assembly-039.question: In RISC-V, what can happen when the address of a 4-byte lw is not a multiple of 4 (misaligned)?
choices: The address is silently rounded to the next multiple of 4 and always read correctly at full speed
Depending on the implementation, it may raise an exception or be handled in hardware or software, possibly very slowly
The low two address bits are simply ignored without error
isa-assembly-039.explanation: A 4-byte item at an address that is a multiple of 4 can be read in one memory access. Crossing a boundary needs two accesses, so RISC-V lets each implementation either handle misaligned accesses in hardware or trap and leave them to software, which can be orders of magnitude slower. This is why compilers insert padding between struct members to keep them aligned.
choiceNotes: The address is never silently changed.
Correct. The ISA allows implementations either way.
Ignoring them would read the wrong location.

isa-assembly-040.question: The RISC-V instruction "slli t0, a0, 3" makes t0 how many times the value of a0 (ignoring overflow)?
choices: 8 times
3 times
6 times
isa-assembly-040.explanation: slli (shift left logical immediate) shifts a register left by the given number of bits and fills the vacated low bits with zeros. In binary, shifting left one bit doubles a value, so three bits multiply by 2^3 = 8. Shifts are often faster than multiply instructions, so compilers replace multiplication by powers of two with shifts. They are also common when computing array element addresses.
choiceNotes: Correct. Shifting left 3 bits multiplies by 2^3.
3 is the shift amount, not the factor.
Each shift doubles the value, so the factors multiply.

isa-assembly-041.question: a0 holds the start address of an int (4-byte) array a, and a1 holds an index i. What does the code above load into a2?
choices: The value of a[4*i]
The address of a[i]
The value of a[i]
isa-assembly-041.explanation: Line 1 shifts i left by 2 bits to get 4 × i, line 2 adds it to the array's start address to get the address of a[i], and line 3 loads 4 bytes from there. Each int is 4 bytes, so element i lies 4 × i bytes from the start. The compiler translates C's "a[i]" into exactly this kind of address calculation followed by a load.
choiceNotes: The address is 4 × i bytes ahead, which is element i.
The final lw loads the value.
Correct. It loads from start + 4 × i.

isa-assembly-042.question: Which statement is correct about designs like x86, where an arithmetic instruction such as "add eax, [rbx]" can use a memory value directly?
choices: Fewer instructions are needed, but one instruction includes both a memory read and an operation
It is called a load-store architecture
Operations on memory values always take the same time as register-to-register ones
isa-assembly-042.explanation: x86 can "load from memory and add" in one instruction, whereas RISC-V needs two, lw and add. Instruction counts and code tend to be smaller, but the amount of work per instruction varies widely, which makes pipelining harder. So today's x86 CPUs internally split such instructions into simple operations (micro-operations), such as a load and an add, and execute those.
choiceNotes: Correct. This is a CISC characteristic.
Load-store designs separate memory access from arithmetic.
The memory read adds time.

isa-assembly-043.question: How do today's high-performance x86 CPUs execute complex instructions internally?
choices: They execute every instruction one at a time in a software emulator
They decode instructions into simple, RISC-like micro-operations and execute those in a pipeline
They cannot run complex instructions, so the OS stops them with an error
isa-assembly-043.explanation: x86 CPUs break variable-length, complex instructions into simple operations called micro-operations (μops) in the front-end decoder, and the back end executes them out of order. Some CPUs keep a μop cache so decoded μops can be reused without decoding again. This lets them keep compatibility with old software while using the same fast execution techniques as RISC designs.
choiceNotes: They are not emulated in software.
Correct. CISC outside, close to RISC inside.
Complex instructions do run.

isa-assembly-044.question: What instructions does the RISC-V M extension add to the base integer instruction set?
choices: Floating-point arithmetic
Atomic instructions
Integer multiplication and division
isa-assembly-044.explanation: RISC-V is a modular ISA that combines a small base integer set (RV32I or RV64I) with whatever extensions are needed. The M extension adds multiply and divide such as mul, div and rem; A adds atomic instructions; F and D add single- and double-precision floating point; and C adds 16-bit compressed instructions. A tiny microcontroller can implement only the base set while a general-purpose CPU includes many extensions.
choiceNotes: Floating point is the F and D extensions.
Atomic instructions are the A extension.
Correct. M stands for multiply.

isa-assembly-045.question: What is the main purpose of the RISC-V C extension (compressed instructions)?
choices: To add instructions that compress data and reduce memory use
To let the CPU run C programs directly
To encode common instructions in 16 bits and make programs smaller
isa-assembly-045.explanation: The C extension represents common instructions in 16-bit forms with restricted fields, for example "addi sp, sp, -16" or lw and sw with small offsets. They mix freely with 32-bit instructions and typically shrink code by about 25-30%. Smaller programs fit more easily in limited flash memory and more of them fit in the instruction cache, which helps both embedded devices and high-performance CPUs.
choiceNotes: It does not compress data.
C stands for compressed, unrelated to the C language.
Correct. Code size shrinks by roughly 25-30%.

isa-assembly-046.question: When C's "a * b" (multiplying two ints) is compiled for an RV32I CPU without the M extension, what generally happens?
choices: It becomes a call to a library function that multiplies by repeated shifts and adds
Multiplication is unavailable, so compilation fails
The M extension's mul instruction is emitted and added automatically at run time
isa-assembly-046.explanation: For CPUs without a multiplier, the compiler replaces multiplication with a call to a helper library function such as __mulsi3. That function computes the product the same way as long multiplication: it examines one operand bit by bit and, for each 1, adds the correspondingly shifted other operand. The answer is correct but tens of times slower than a hardware multiplier. Omitting an ISA extension makes the circuit smaller at the cost of slower processing.
choiceNotes: Correct. Software does the work instead of hardware.
C multiplication works for any target CPU.
Executing a nonexistent instruction raises an illegal-instruction exception.

isa-assembly-047.question: What is true of the branch delay slot found in older ISAs such as MIPS (the rule that the one instruction right after a branch always executes, taken or not)?
choices: It makes branch prediction 100% accurate and is essential in today's CPUs
RISC-V adopts it too, so a nop must follow every branch
It exposed a quirk of the pipelines of its time in the ISA and later became a burden for CPU designs
isa-assembly-047.explanation: In a simple five-stage pipeline, the next instruction has already been fetched by the time a branch resolves, so the delay slot made it always execute to avoid waste. In later CPUs with deep pipelines, branch prediction and multiple issue, the benefit vanished and only the burden of special handling for compatibility remained. RISC-V avoids it so as not to bake implementation-dependent rules into the ISA.
choiceNotes: It is not branch prediction and is unnecessary today.
RISC-V does not have branch delay slots.
Correct. It froze a microarchitectural detail into the ISA.

isa-assembly-048.question: On 64-bit RV64I, how does lw place the 32-bit value it loads into a 64-bit register?
choices: The upper 32 bits keep their old value and only the lower 32 bits change
It is always zero-extended to 64 bits
It is sign-extended to 64 bits (lwu is used for zero extension)
isa-assembly-048.explanation: On RV64I, lw sign-extends the 32-bit value into the 64-bit register, while lwu, the unsigned load, fills the upper bits with zeros. Leaving the old upper bits in place would create a dependence on the previous value and hinder out-of-order execution, so RISC-V never does that. For 32-bit arithmetic there are instructions with a "w" suffix such as addw, which compute a 32-bit result and then sign-extend it.
choiceNotes: RISC-V never leaves the old upper bits in place.
Zero extension is the lwu instruction.
Correct. It treats the value as a signed 32-bit number.

isa-assembly-049.question: Which correctly describes an ABI (application binary interface)?
choices: An agreement at the source-code level defining function names and argument types
An agreement defining only the kinds of CPU instructions and their bit layouts
A set of machine-level agreements, such as calling conventions and data type sizes and alignment, that let programs interoperate
isa-assembly-049.explanation: An ABI is the machine-level agreement that lets compiled programs and libraries work together. It covers the calling convention, the sizes of int, long and pointers, struct alignment, how system calls are made and so on. An API defines how functions are used at the source level; even with the same API, a different ABI means a library cannot be used without rebuilding. The same RISC-V ISA can have different ABIs depending on the OS or application.
choiceNotes: That is an API (application programming interface).
That is the ISA; the ABI sits on top of it.
Correct. It is an agreement between compiled pieces of code.

isa-assembly-050.question: How is a call through a C function pointer, "(*fp)(x)", generally performed in RISC-V?
choices: The function address is placed in a register, and jalr jumps to that register's address
jal jumps with the function address written as an immediate
beq compares with the function address and jumps if equal
isa-assembly-050.explanation: The target of a function pointer is not known until run time, so jal, whose target is written in the instruction, cannot be used. Instead the pointer value is loaded into a register and the code jumps to it with, for example, "jalr ra, 0(t0)", leaving the return address in ra. Calls to C++ virtual functions and shared-library functions are similar indirect calls. Because the target can change, CPUs predict it with an indirect branch predictor.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is an indirect call whose target is set at run time.
jal's target is fixed in the instruction and cannot change at run time.
beq is a conditional branch, not used for calls.
